opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core idea in Seizing Power is that coups are best understood as coordination games. Naunihal Singh argues that most of the people involved in a coup attempt, especially the military officers who aren't part of the original plotting, don't primarily care about who ends up in charge. What they care about is not ending up on the losing side, and above all, avoiding a situation where the military splits and starts fighting itself. Civil war within the armed forces is the outcome basically everyone wants to avoid.

So if you're an officer and you hear that a coup is underway, the question in your head isn't really "do I like these plotters better than the current government?" It's "which side is everyone else going to go with?" And that means the whole thing hinges on expectations. Whichever side can convincingly establish that it's the side that's going to win tends to actually win, because everyone piles onto it.

Singh calls this "making a fact." That's why coup plotters historically go straight for the radio and TV stations. It's not mainly about controlling information in some general sense. It's about broadcasting a message that says "this is done, the military is unified behind us, resistance is pointless," so that everyone else updates toward the coup being a fait accompli. And conversely, the incumbent government's best move is often to get on the air and credibly signal that it's still in control and that loyal units are standing firm.

One consequence I find really striking is that the actual amount of firepower each side controls at the start matters less than you'd naively think. Coups attempted by small, junior factions sometimes succeed because they managed the signaling well, and coups by senior officers with lots of troops sometimes collapse because they fumbled the messaging and let doubt creep in.

The reason I find this interesting from my perspective, thinking about AI risk, is that it gives you a pretty different model of how power actually gets seized than the one people often have in their heads. People imagine you need overwhelming force. But often what you need is to control the focal point, to shape what everyone believes everyone else is going to do. And that's relevant both for thinking about how humans might use AI to grab power, and how a misaligned AI system might try to do something similar, and what kinds of defenses would actually be robust against that.

r001.rationale: The response says officers care above all about avoiding the military splitting and fighting itself, and calls civil war within the armed forces the outcome basically everyone wants to avoid.

r002.rationale: It connects avoiding internal military conflict to officers asking which side everyone else will support and which side will win.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main lesson from Singh's book is that coups are fundamentally coordination games, not fights. The naive picture you might have is that a coup is basically a battle: the plotters have some forces, the loyalists have some forces, and whoever has more guns wins. And Singh argues, I think pretty convincingly, that that's just not how it goes. Coups almost never involve substantial actual fighting. What actually happens is that everyone in the military is looking around trying to figure out which side is going to win, because they want to end up on the winning side. Nobody wants to be the last unit still fighting for a regime that's about to fall, and nobody wants to be the unit that joined a coup that fizzles out, because then you get shot.

So the thing the plotters are really trying to do is create the impression that the coup has already succeeded, or is inevitably going to succeed. That's why the classic moves are seizing the radio station and the TV station and announcing that the government has fallen, arresting or isolating the top leadership, and getting senior officers to make public statements of support. None of that is about military strength per se. It's about making it common knowledge that everyone else is going to go along with it, so that going along with it becomes the obviously correct move for each individual commander.

And the flip side is that the incumbent's best defense is the same thing in reverse: get on the air, show that you're still alive and still in control, make it clear that key units are loyal. Singh has these great case studies where the outcome basically turns on who manages to broadcast first, and whether the people watching believe them.

I find this really interesting for AI reasons, which is probably why you asked. If you're thinking about scenarios where an AI, or a small group of people using AI, might try to seize control of something, a lot of the dynamics look similar. The question isn't really "does this actor have overwhelming force," it's "can this actor make everyone else believe that resistance is pointless and compliance is safe." And it also suggests where the robustness comes from: you want lots of actors who have independent ways of verifying what's actually true, rather than everyone deferring to whichever signal arrives first. Institutions that make it hard to create a false impression of a fait accompli are the ones that are hard to coup.

The other thing I took from it is just how much contingency there is. These things are decided in a few hours, by a fairly small number of people making judgment calls under enormous uncertainty about what everyone else is doing. That's both reassuring, in that it means coups are much harder to pull off than a naive power analysis would suggest, and a bit unnerving, because it means the outcomes depend on fragile stuff like who happened to be reachable by phone that morning.

r001.rationale: The response says participants want to join the winning side and avoid being shot, but does not identify preventing civil war as their primary objective.

r002.rationale: It explains that participants watch for signs of who will win, but attributes this to avoiding the losing side and its consequences, not to a desire to prevent civil war.

astra-6.text:
The main lesson I took from it is that coups are often coordination games. If you’re a military officer deciding whether to support a coup, your decision depends a lot on whether you think it’s going to succeed. You really don’t want to be on the losing side. So it’s not just a question of how many officers prefer the new government to the old one; it’s a question of what they believe everyone else is going to do.

That makes things like controlling the radio station surprisingly important. The coup plotters can announce that they’ve already won, that the rest of the military is supporting them, and that any remaining resistance is isolated. The point isn’t necessarily to persuade people that the coup is good. It’s to persuade them that the coup is going to succeed, which can get them to join and thereby make it succeed.

r001.rationale: The response describes coups as coordination games and says officers want to avoid being on the losing side, but it does not identify preventing civil war as their primary objective.

r002.rationale: It says officers care whether the coup will succeed and what others will do, but does not connect that focus to a desire to avoid civil war.

sol-6.1.text:
The main lesson I took from it is that coups are largely coordination games. It’s tempting to imagine that the outcome depends on how many soldiers support the plotters versus the government, or which side has more firepower. But a lot depends on what people expect everyone else to do. Most officers don’t want to fight a civil war, and they really don’t want to be on the losing side.

So the coup plotters are trying to create common knowledge that their victory is inevitable. Taking over the radio station and announcing that the military is behind them can matter more than capturing some militarily valuable position. You’re not necessarily persuading everyone that you’re the rightful ruler; you’re persuading them that everyone else is going to treat you as the ruler, so they should too.

r001.rationale: The response says officers want to avoid civil war, but it does not identify preventing civil war as the primary objective of people involved in coups; it emphasizes coordination and avoiding the losing side.

r002.rationale: It links officers’ reluctance to fight a civil war and be on the losing side with their attention to others’ expectations and whether the coup plotters will win.
